title: The Merck/Moderna Results
body_text: This is one of those times - and there are many - when you should evaluate a biopharma news story based on the science and not on the stock market. I’m referring to the clinical trial data that Merck and Moderna released yesterday for their vaccine (intismeran autogene)/Keytruda combination in melanoma patients after surgery. That should probably read “released under duress”, because the data leaked in advance of a meeting presentation, and the companies were more or less forced to press-release on the numbers. There will be more details on Saturday during the actual presentation. We already had a bit of a preview back in August saying that the interim Phase III readout showd “a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement”, and that the trial had met its primary endpoint (recurrence-free survival). And earlier the Phase II results were a 49% lower rate of recurrence or death in the treatment group. The Phase III data announced yesterday were right in line with all these, actually, with a 42% reduction in the risk or death or recurrence of melanoma (after a median follow-up of two years). Keytruda, it has to be said, is a hard standard to beat in melanoma patients: after two years, 70% of the Keytruda-alone patients had not relapsed. But 82.2% of the combination treatment group had not. And it’s worth pointing out that the overall survival numbers are still counting up at this point. Keytruda is a fantastic drug, and it’s very impressive that another immunological treatment could actually add to its benefit. Both Merck and Moderna’s stocks took quite a hit on this news, though. That’s got to be partly the “buy on the hype and sell on the news” strategy that one sees all the time, and it’s also (I would have to think) some people who were getting ahead of the science on this one and hoping for what the British tabloids have called for years, a “cancer superjab!” The other thing to remember that that both stocks have been running up all year based on the earlier news, and were arguably too high for any reasonable numbers out of this trial to support. This combination is in fact being tested in several other forms of cancer right now, and we’re just going to have to wait for the data to see how much improvement there is. Bladder and renal cell carcinoma look like the first two that we’ll see. But given how long people have been trying to get a therapeutic-vaccine approach to work in any form of cancer, this is a really significant result. It’s also a lot of work: intiserman is personalized to each patient depending on their neoantigen profile from their particular tumor, and there’s a list of up to 34 possible neoantigens in the mix, each as an mRNA construct in the vaccine dose. This is an expensive way to do it, but in the current state of the art it’s the way we have. I fully expect this technique to work better on some forms of cancer than others, and inside each type, for it to work better on some patients than others. This hardly needs to be said for those of us who work in drug discovery or oncology therapies, but it would be a good thing for the general public to take in (and apparently a good thing for investors to realize as well!) But the other thing to take in is that it really is a significant step forward in the long-running efforts to turn the immune system into an anticancer weapon. That “long-running” part also means that this is all still going on, and will be going on for many, many years to come. There are uncountable things that we don’t understand about the immune system and about the behavior of tumor cells. There is a huge amount of work to be done. The fact that we’re seeing results like this now is very much a reason to hope that even better things are coming.
